source_text: Omnis quippe, ut ait ille, quae ratione suscipitur de aliqua re disputatio, debet a definitione proficisci, ut intellegatur quid sit id de quo disputatur [n184] . Ita ergo et nos, sicut supra de iustitiae et peccati definitione disseruimus, nunc quoque videamus quae libertati arbitrii definitio competat ut planum sit, quis ei nostrum consentiat, quis repugnet. Libertas arbitrii, qua a Deo emancipatus homo est, in admittendi peccati et abstinendi a peccato possibilitate consistit.
pass_a_gloss: For every, as that man says, disputation about some thing which is taken up by reason, ought to set out from a definition, that it may be understood what that is about which it is disputed. So therefore also we, as above we discussed about the definition of justice and of sin, now too let us see which definition is competent to the liberty of choice, that it may be plain who of us consents to it, who fights. The liberty of choice, by which the human has been emancipated by God, consists in the possibility of admitting sin and of abstaining from sin.

lemmas.lexica: LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS arbitrium=judgment, free decision; Blaise liberum arbitrium
LS libertas; Blaise moral freedom to will or refuse
LS ratio; Blaise use of reason required for sin
LS possibilitas; Blaise capacity to will

pass_b_english: For, as the author says, “Every discussion of a subject undertaken rationally ought to begin with a definition, so that what is being discussed may be understood” (Cicero, On Duties 1.7). Thus, just as we discussed the definitions of justice and sin above, let us now consider what definition belongs to freedom of choice, so that it may be clear which of us agrees with it and which opposes it. Freedom of choice, by which God gave the human being independence, consists in the capacity to commit sin and to abstain from sin.

choices.why: Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.
Glossary default: arbitrium is the decision-power, not a later Augustinian/Reformation free-will locus.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
